speaker: GOD
text: Where are you?

speaker: GUIDE
text: The last chapter ended with a man and a woman, naked and unashamed, in a very good world. This chapter answers the question every reader eventually asks. If the world began like that, why is it like this? It begins with a question. Not God's question. Another voice asks first.

speaker: READER
text: Now the serpent was more crafty than any beast of the field that the LORD God had made. And he said to the woman, “Did God really say, ‘You must not eat from any tree in the garden?’”

speaker: GUIDE
text: The chapter opens with a pun English cannot keep. The pair were naked, arummim. The serpent is crafty, arum. The two words sound almost the same.

speaker: GUIDE
text: The people who first heard this had just come out of Egypt, where a rearing cobra crowned Pharaoh's head. In that world the snake meant wisdom, healing, power. Genesis refuses to make it a god. It is a creature the LORD God had made, and it ends this chapter eating dust.

speaker: GUIDE
text: Later Scripture names the voice behind it:

speaker: READER
text: that ancient serpent called the devil and Satan

speaker: GUIDE
text: Jesus calls him

speaker: READER
text: the father of lies

speaker: GUIDE
text: And watch how he works. He never commands. He only asks. His first move is a question about what God said.

speaker: READER
text: The woman answered the serpent, “We may eat the fruit of the trees of the garden,

speaker: READER
text: but about the fruit of the tree in the middle of the garden, God has said, ‘You must not eat of it or touch it, or you will die.’”

speaker: READER
text: “You will not surely die,” the serpent told the woman.

speaker: READER
text: “For God knows that in the day you eat of it, your eyes will be opened and you will be like God, knowing good and evil.”

speaker: GUIDE
text: Lay the two side by side and you can watch the lie being built. God said, eat freely from every tree, with one limit and a clear warning. She drops the freely, adds touching, and softens the warning. She shrinks the gift and enlarges the limit.

speaker: GUIDE
text: Then the serpent takes God's own words and puts a not in front of them. He contradicts God word for word, and he paints the Giver of every tree as jealous, holding something good back.

speaker: GUIDE
text: Notice too that the narrator says the LORD God, His covenant name. In this conversation they say only God. The personal name drops out just as trust in Him is dissolving.

speaker: GUIDE
text: The root of sin, as Genesis tells it, is not ignorance. It is distrust. A willingness to believe that God is holding back something good, and that His word can be edited.

speaker: READER
text: When the woman saw that the tree was good for food and pleasing to the eyes, and that it was desirable for obtaining wisdom, she took the fruit and ate it. She also gave some to her husband who was with her, and he ate it.

speaker: READER
text: And the eyes of both of them were opened, and they knew that they were naked; so they sewed together fig leaves and made coverings for themselves.

speaker: GUIDE
text: This is the only window the narrator gives into her mind, and it climbs. Good for food: the appetite. Pleasing to the eyes: the eye. Desirable for wisdom: ambition.

speaker: GUIDE
text: Desirable is the verb of the tenth commandment.

speaker: READER
text: You shall not covet

speaker: GUIDE
text: What God made to be enjoyed becomes something to be seized. And the man was with her the whole time, saying nothing at all.

speaker: GUIDE
text: Their eyes are opened, as the serpent promised. But what they see is their own exposure. One act fractures every relationship at once. They hide from God, they cover themselves from each other, and the fig leaves are their own attempt to fix it.

speaker: READER
text: Then the man and his wife heard the voice of the LORD God walking in the garden in the breeze of the day, and they hid themselves from the presence of the LORD God among the trees of the garden.

speaker: READER
text: But the LORD God called out to the man,

speaker: GOD
text: “Where are you?”

speaker: READER
text: “I heard Your voice in the garden,” he replied, “and I was afraid because I was naked; so I hid myself.”

speaker: GUIDE
text: Walking is the very word Israel would later use for God's presence moving through their camp. Their sanctuary was a garden like this one. And here, the man and the woman hide from Him among the trees He planted.

speaker: GUIDE
text: Many readers see this question as the centre of the whole chapter. The turning point is not the eating. It is the God who comes looking. He knows where they are. He asks so that the guilty will speak the truth, as He later asks Cain,

speaker: READER
text: Where is your brother Abel?

speaker: GUIDE
text: and Elijah,

speaker: READER
text: What are you doing here?

speaker: GUIDE
text: God's first word to fallen humanity is not a sentence. It is a search.

chapter: The woman whom You gave me
speaker: GOD
text: “Who told you that you were naked?”

chapter: The woman whom You gave me
speaker: READER
text: asked the LORD God.

chapter: The woman whom You gave me
speaker: GOD
text: “Have you eaten from the tree of which I commanded you not to eat?”

chapter: The woman whom You gave me
speaker: READER
text: And the man answered, “The woman whom You gave me, she gave me fruit from the tree, and I ate it.”

chapter: The woman whom You gave me
speaker: READER
text: Then the LORD God said to the woman,

chapter: The woman whom You gave me
speaker: GOD
text: “What is this you have done?”

chapter: The woman whom You gave me
speaker: READER
text: “The serpent deceived me,” she replied, “and I ate.”

chapter: The woman whom You gave me
speaker: GUIDE
text: Look at the shape of it. The sin travels from serpent to woman to man. God's questions run the other way, man then woman, and the blame is passed back down the line. The sentences will retrace the first order.

chapter: The woman whom You gave me
speaker: GUIDE
text: The man said nothing until he was questioned, and now he speaks to excuse himself. The woman whom You gave me. What she says is true, but it is not a defence.

chapter: The woman whom You gave me
speaker: GUIDE
text: And God puts no question to the serpent. He does not negotiate with evil. He sentences it.

speaker: READER
text: So the LORD God said to the serpent:

speaker: GOD
text: “Because you have done this, cursed are you above all livestock and every beast of the field! On your belly will you go, and dust you will eat, all the days of your life.

speaker: GUIDE
text: Cursed falls on the serpent and on the ground, never on the man or the woman themselves. And even in Isaiah's renewed world, this one sentence still stands:

speaker: READER
text: the food of the serpent will be dust

speaker: GOD
text: And I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your seed and her seed. He will crush your head, and you will strike his heel.”

speaker: GUIDE
text: Enmity means open war. The rescue of the world begins as God's own declaration of war on evil.

speaker: GUIDE
text: One verb stands behind both blows, the head and the heel. The difference is the target: a fatal blow against a wounding one. And the seed is he. Even the old Greek translators heard a person in this promise. A long war between two lines, but the decisive blow is struck by one.

speaker: GUIDE
text: This is the first announcement of the gospel, and it is spoken before a single sentence falls on the man and the woman.

speaker: READER
text: To the woman He said:

speaker: GOD
text: “I will sharply increase your pain in childbirth; in pain you will bring forth children. Your desire will be for your husband, and he will rule over you.”

speaker: GUIDE
text: Her pain is the same word as the man's toil: the sentence falls on both in the same currency. And the desire and the rule describe a marriage bent by sin, not God's design. It is a sorrowful description of the world under judgment, never a charter for it.

speaker: READER
text: And to Adam He said:

speaker: GOD
text: “Because you have listened to the voice of your wife and have eaten from the tree of which I commanded you not to eat, cursed is the ground because of you; through toil you will eat of it all the days of your life.

speaker: GOD
text: Both thorns and thistles it will yield for you, and you will eat the plants of the field.

speaker: GOD
text: By the sweat of your brow you will eat your bread, until you return to the ground, because out of it were you taken. For dust you are, and to dust you shall return.”

speaker: GUIDE
text: Chapter two ran from dust to a living man. Chapter three runs that film backward. The man taken from the ground will return to it. And from here a refrain tolls through Genesis, beginning with Adam himself:

speaker: READER
text: and then he died

speaker: GUIDE
text: Yet mercy is laced through the judgment. Childbearing goes on, so the promised seed can still come. Work goes on, so life goes on. Judgment is real, but it is bounded.

speaker: READER
text: And Adam named his wife Eve, because she would be the mother of all the living.

speaker: GUIDE
text: Eve sounds like the Hebrew for living. In the very hour death enters, he names her the mother of all the living. A small act of hope in God's promise.

speaker: READER
text: And the LORD God made garments of skin for Adam and his wife, and He clothed them.

speaker: GUIDE
text: The fig leaves were their own covering. These garments are God's. And the words are the ones used when Moses clothed Israel's priests. The brick-maker would have watched it happen: tunics, the same word, put on by another's hands.

speaker: GUIDE
text: The text does not describe a sacrifice, so the link is an inference, but a fair one. The covering came from a life taken.

speaker: READER
text: Then the LORD God said,

speaker: GOD
text: “Behold, the man has become like one of Us, knowing good and evil. And now, lest he reach out his hand and take also from the tree of life, and eat, and live forever...”

speaker: GUIDE
text: Even the exile is a mercy. It guards them from living forever in a fallen state.

speaker: READER
text: Therefore the LORD God banished him from the Garden of Eden to work the ground from which he had been taken.

speaker: READER
text: So He drove out the man and stationed cherubim on the east side of the Garden of Eden, along with a whirling sword of flame to guard the way to the tree of life.

speaker: GUIDE
text: Stationed is the verb of God's dwelling, the root of the word for the tabernacle. The guard that keeps sinners out is described in the language of God's house.

speaker: GUIDE
text: To Israel this sounded like being barred from the sanctuary. Its door faced east, and cherubim were woven into the veil before the Most Holy Place. No one simply walked back in.

speaker: GUIDE
text: And Israel heard its own story in Adam. Given a good land and one word to keep, warned of death, they disobeyed, and they too were carried east, into exile in Babylon. Hosea says they

speaker: READER
text: like Adam, have transgressed the covenant

speaker: GUIDE
text: East becomes a direction in Genesis. Cain settles east of Eden. The builders of Babel journey east. Humanity keeps moving away from the presence it lost.

speaker: GUIDE
text: Verse fifteen never names the victor, and the rest of the Bible keeps watching for him. The promise narrows to Abraham, then to David, and comes to rest on one person. God sent His Son, Paul says,

speaker: READER
text: born of a woman

speaker: GUIDE
text: Luke traces Jesus back to

speaker: READER
text: the son of Adam, the son of God

speaker: GUIDE
text: and the very next scene is the temptation. The last Adam meets the same enemy, in a wilderness instead of a garden, hungry instead of surrounded by fruit. The serpent began by questioning what God said. Jesus answers with what God said:

speaker: READER
text: It is written

speaker: GUIDE
text: Adam hid among the trees. Christ was hung on a tree. Adam reached for what was forbidden. Christ, in a garden, prayed,

speaker: READER
text: not as I will, but as You will

speaker: GUIDE
text: Adam wore thorns as the fruit of his sin. Christ wore them as a crown. Adam left the garden to die. Christ was laid in a garden tomb, and rose. The promise never pictured a victory without cost. He shared our flesh and blood,

speaker: READER
text: so that by His death He might destroy him who holds the power of death

speaker: GUIDE
text: The strike to the heel and the crushing of the head happen in the same act.

speaker: GUIDE
text: The cherubim that barred the way to life stood again over the mercy seat in Israel's sanctuary, where God promised,

speaker: READER
text: I will meet with you there

speaker: GUIDE
text: The guard at the door of Eden became the throne of atonement. And when Jesus died, the veil with its cherubim was torn from top to bottom. Believers now come in

speaker: READER
text: by the new and living way opened for us through the curtain of His body

speaker: GUIDE
text: The Bible closes by undoing this chapter. No longer any curse. The tree of life open beside the river. And the pair who hid from God among the trees are answered by a people who

speaker: READER
text: will see His face

speaker: GUIDE
text: So hear God's questions as grace. The right answer to His question is not to hide and not to blame. It is to come out, confess, and trust the God who promised a Rescuer and clothed the naked.

speaker: GUIDE
text: God covered their shame with garments He provided. What are you using to cover your own shame, and what would it mean to receive God's covering in Christ instead?

speaker: GUIDE
text: East of Eden, the first children are born. Two brothers bring offerings to God. And the next time God comes asking a question, it will be about a brother.
